utterances.text: Milorad Ulemek at that time was in charge. He was the commander of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, and he was in charge of them in that operation that we were engaged in in Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please play the remainder of the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, sir, could you please watch and listen to the contents of the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "What do you need? Tell me. Goose. Goose. What do you need? Tell me. Gooska, what do you need? Tell me. What do you need, Gooska? "Down, down, Branko, down. In the left part, yes, in the left part. I still have small problems with the right one. "Well, go to hell. Give me, where is my Motorola? "From this first house here. Come on and get. All right. In that white house right from that one, that stable, and that hay there, there where there is that trench. "The white one, the biggest one? "Yes, yes. I need a team to be sent here to take over. There are five from 205. "What idiots are they for fucks sake? They are idiots. Who has brought them over here? Idiots. "Come on, call Azim to send a team -- where? At Grmec? "Yes. "At Grmec to the command post to pick up a parcel. "Fuck you and the parcel. "They should kill them. "Orkan, come in. "Tell me, Orkan, come in, tell me, I'm listening. "Well, we only need one. "Well, fuck you. All right, all right, I solved it. "Well, you try it just like that."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, in the video that you just watched which I belive now has ended at the 3 minute and 20 second marker. There's a reference to Orkan, could you please explain what that is?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Orkan is a military piece. It is a multi-rocket-launcher. And in this video-clip we can see that from Grmec position they requested support, artillery support, or the other way around. Grmec is an artillery position. Like, for example, in the American, Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, we in the Yugoslavia army --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Avala, Grmec, so G would stand for Grmec.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the content of this video, can you tell what the location is of this operation?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I can see a trench. And judging by the date, I would say that this corresponds to the period when operations were underway in Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the communications equipment that was used throughout this video-clip, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Motorola radios, ZGP 300, we had the same type of communications equipment in our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time tenders into evidence of the video-clip from 65 ter 1180. If we could tender the full 3 minute and 20 second clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No. Madam Registrar, the video-clip would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P483, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P483 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Weber --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you -- could I first ask you, are you more or less on track as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm a little bit behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There is still not the resolution of the per diem list, so without knowing that, I should be able to progress through my remaining examination in the next half-hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How does our schedule look for the coming days? We had three days this week, if I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct. The Prosecution will finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Then I believe that we do not know how much time will be needed for cross-examination of this witness. And then I believe that the Chamber had raised a question about next Tuesday which is not yet resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but is there any other witness waiting for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have today and tomorrow. Could I receive an indication as to the time needed for cross-examination of this witness? Mr. Knoops?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Approximately one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One hour and a half. Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that I will not need more than an hour and a half altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. You may use another half-hour, and we'll then look at the per diem lists as a separate issue as far as time is concerned. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see Legija in Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had a number of occasions to see him because he came very often. He visited the place where we were billeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any conversations between Legija and Franko Simatovic or Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I was standing guard when I heard a conversation which was taking place in the office between Franko Simatovic and Milorad Ulemek Legija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please describe this conversation?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Milorad Ulemek wanted to take over the operation to take Kladusa. I don't know which one, the Velika or the Mala. And he wanted to transfer some of the troops from Lemici and Popovic Brdo, and he said that he would be able to mount a frontal attack and take that position in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you hear if Franko Simatovic said anything in response to Legija's request?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he said, Okay, everything will be as we agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately when did this conversation occur?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date, but it was sometime in November, in the second half of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Based on the interactions that you observed between Legija and Franko Simatovic and Jovica Stanisic, could you please describe them?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to what I heard, one could tell from the type of conversation that Milorad Ulemek was subordinated to Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic. I could tell by the way they talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 50 of Exhibit P441, you indicate that Fikret Abdic arrived for meetings with Stanisic and Simatovic while you were in Petrova Gora. How often did you see Fikret Abdic meet with Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: He came and I saw him on several occasions when he came to the office to talk to them. I can't give you the dates. I can't tell you how often, but I'm sure that I saw him two, three, or even four times when he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 49 of Exhibit P441, you describe two meetings that you observed between Milan Martic and Stanisic and Simatovic. Could you please describe each of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't present during the meeting. I know that they came to the command post where we were. On two occasions I saw them. On the first one they came altogether at the same time in their vehicles, and on the second occasion they came separately. And I'm referring to Ratko Mladic and Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your statement you refer to Ratko Mladic coming in December of 1994 during the second meeting of -- with Milan Martic. Could you please describe the exchange that occurred between Ratko Mladic's men and the members of the Red Berets who were on duty?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I was standing on the terrace with a person whose nickname was Njegos; he was a member of our unit. I was getting ready to go home. Can I please look at the part of the statement where I stated that? I would like to look at my own words, the way I described the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I think the most --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's paragraph 49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The most appropriate way of dealing with it is first to elicit what the witness remembers. And if there's any need to refresh his memory, so -- but let's not start by refreshing the memory. And I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I may read the statement, consistent with 92 ter practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's -- I know that it is, but let's first -- yes. Could you first tell us what your recollection is. And if there are details you may have forgotten about, then we'll further look perhaps at your statement. So could you please -- you started answering a -- the question by saying that you were standing on the terrace with a person whose nickname was, and then you mentioned his nickname, being a member of your unit, and you were getting ready to go home. Could you please continue to describe the exchange that occurred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was standing with Negos. Mladic approached us, and he said, Why are you in civilian clothes? At that time I didn't know who he was, and I told him, Fatso, mind your own business. After that, they entered the office where he was. Stojan Zupljanin came with them. I spoke to Stojan Zupljanin's guards and his driver. His name was Branko Simic, and the other was Predrag Brestovac. And there was another man whose nickname was Vuha [phoen]. And they told me that they had arrived from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraphs 62 and 63 of Exhibit P441, you discuss your service in Tara as a member of the Red Berets. In paragraph 63 you state: "Members of the unit used the gym and swimming pool of the Omorika Hotel for training." Where is the Omorika Hotel located in Tara?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: The hotel at Tara where the unit was billeted was a separate facility with a complete infrastructure as any other small size hotel. It was about 3 and a half kilometres away from hotel Omorika, and it looked like a lower-category facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have ERN 0675-6870A. This is a photograph that was provided to the OTP in proofing in April and shown to the Defence prior to the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may I first seek clarification. You said "with a complete infrastructure as any other small size hotel." Now, sometimes I find complete infrastructures in large hotels rather than in the small ones. Is that what your testimony is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to describe the hotel, and I wanted to tell you that the hotel looked as any other. The personnel of that hotel was similar to any other hotel. It didn't have a swimming pool or any other such things, but it had accommodation facilities, there was a laundry room, there was a kitchen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm rather confused. The question was: "Where is the Omorika Hotel located in Tara?" Then you said: "The hotel at Tara where the unit was billeted was a separate facility with a complete infrastructure as any other small size hotel." And then you say: "It was about 3 and a half kilometres away from the hotel Omorika." So when you were asked to describe the location of the Om orika Hotel, you apparently described the location or the facilities of a hotel other than Omorika. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we were billeted in a motel whose name was Tara. Our training took place in a different A-category hotel which had a swimming pool as well. And that hotel, the latter, was called Omorika.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that explains the confusion. Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see a photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Djordje Kuburovic and myself. That was Djordje Kuburovic's room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: This photo was taken in the Tara facility where we were billeted, where we slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just so we have a clear record, are you located on the right or left in this photograph, as you are looking at it?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm on the right-hand side of the photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can you please describe the weapons that you are holding?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a machine-gun PKT-7.62 x 54 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you receive this weapon?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I received this weapon as part of the unit's armament. Actually, this machine-gun was issued to Desimir Butkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you then acquire it at some later point?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: No. At the time, I had a standard automatic rifle 7.62 and the rocket-launcher, but for the purpose of this photo I took Desimir Butkovic's machine-gun and that's how the photo was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please describe the equipment depicted on the lower left-hand side of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see uniforms that we were issued with. You can see the colour of the uniform, black and blue, which were used by Special Police Units. And in the back you see back-packs used by the American army. And most of those back-packs bore the insignia standing for the United States, US. Behind me there are boots, Gortex boots, which were very expensive at the time, and ankle boots that we used in confined spaces for assaults and anti-terrorist activities and for helicopter actions. This is all the equipment that we were issued with during training at Surcin Airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Photograph under the 65 ter 5315 becomes Exhibit P484, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the end of May 1995, what was the reason that you decided to leave the JATD?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Zvezdan Jovanovic was appointed the unit commander, and he brought a man who was in charge of us. I can't remember his name. I stood guard by a tree for 10 to 12 hours as a disciplinary measure, and I could no longer bear that psychologically. I filed a request to leave the unit. I handed it over. I returned all the equipment at the Tara hotel, and I returned to Belgrade. Dragan Krsmanovic asked me how come I left everything in Tara since I was not issued with the equipment there, and he said that Zvezdan Jovanovic could not have received any equipment from me, that it could only be done by the person who had issued the equipment to me in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 63 of Exhibit P441 you state that you were later told that you should leave the 72nd Brigade and you went to the Belgrade headquarters of the Serb Volunteer Guard. What is the reason that you were told to leave the 72nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: The then-commander who was my superior in the 72nd Special Brigade where I started working after having left that unit told me that he did not want to have any former members of that unit in the 72nd Brigade. And they sent me to Mount Avala. And I was met there by a security officer who then questioned me about Operation Pauk in Velika Kladusa. He didn't actually have many questions about why I was leaving the 72nd Brigade and who had sent me. I was told at the time that they already knew that I had been a member of that unit even before they heard it from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You indicate that you subsequently went to the headquarters of the Serbian Volunteer Guard after leaving the 72nd Brigade. How did you know where the headquarters of the Serb Volunteer Guard was located in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: It was generally known that in the headquarters of the Party of Serb Unity at Beograd Utica Street there was the reception centre for volunteers who wanted to join the Serb Volunteers Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You say it was generally known. Who generally knew the location of the headquarters of the party of the Serb Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: The people I communicated with at the time. There were a number of them who were already members of the Serb Volunteers Guard, and they told me. So I meant the people around me. Milic is the last name of one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is the name that the Serb Volunteer Guard is commonly known by to you?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: They were called Arkan's Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During your time in Erdut and Klisa, did you see any members of the SDG who you knew from your time in Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Big Rambo, who -- he was at Velika Kladusa, and he was Sarac. He was a captain at the time. I met him, and he even gave me a permit to go home. So he signed my permit to leave the area where I was at the time, that was the camp at Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have ERN 0675-6869.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I further inquire. You said you saw Big Rambo. He was at Velika Kladusa. And what did you then say? And he was ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was one of the commanders of the Serbian Volunteers Guard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know his real name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that his last name is Bujosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was taken in the village of Klisa. This is me and two members of the SDG who were not members of my platoon. This was an abandoned house. We found the personal documents of an elderly woman. We simply took the opportunity to take a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where are you depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm the one who is standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of the two individuals who are sitting?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the names. I only had my photograph taken with them then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you -- I am sorry, was there something you wanted to --

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to them, and I could tell by their speech that they were not from Serbia. They must have been from some other area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was this photograph taken during your service in the SDG?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was taken at some time in 1995 in early December.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar, the number would be -- because I see it's uploaded as one out of a series of five. You just want to tender this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, and there will be one more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The photograph you -- the earlier one was also one out of a series of five, so we are getting --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't realise that they had all been uploaded together. I thought that they were separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because the two persons in the room is number 4 out of 5. Now, you want to have them separately --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The -- if we could, actually, because he is describing them individually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the previous one, therefore, is the fourth page out of five from the uploaded 65 ter number, whereas the present one is the second page out of five as uploaded. Madam Registrar, this --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So fourth page of 65 ter 5315 becomes Exhibit P484, just for the record. And page 2 of the 65 ter 5315 becomes Exhibit P485, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in order to avoid whatever confusion, P485 is ERN 0675-6869, whereas P484 is ERN 0675-6870A. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 1 of 65 ter 5315, which is ERN 0675-6868.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This photograph was taken at Erdut. This is behind the reception facility for new recruits. Upstairs there was a cafeteria. This is a platoon of the SDG which I -- to which I was assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this was late October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this photograph is deliberately blurred. I'm squatting on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It might be easiest if we actually -- if the witness could be, please, provided a pen, and the Prosecution will ask the witness to circle his location in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders the screen capture that has been marked by the witness into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P486, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, photograph marked by the witness, P486 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you receive any type of payments as a member of the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the Red Berets, yes, I received a salary and per diems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did these payments begin?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: As members of the unit, we started receiving salaries -- well, I actually think that we received something upfront from May on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you refer to May, May of what year?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about May 1994. Actually, no, I apologise, June 1994. That's when I started receiving my salary and the per diems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How did you receive these payments?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: We received our salaries in cash. The cash was in envelopes. And we signed pay slips that we had received the salaries and the per diems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if you are running out of time, isn't this in the statement as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is. And I'm almost finished, actually, Your Honour, with my entire examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please -- it is in the statement. Just so we have it on the record though, could you describe these envelopes?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: They were specific envelopes that I only saw at these two places, either at the JATD or at the SDG. There was a -- like, a table on the back side of the envelope. The same kind that you would find enclosed with your chequebook. And the table was blue, whereas the envelopes themselves were white.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How many payments did you receive as a member of the SDG?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Three times. I got three salaries. The first salary wasn't paid out in full because I had only yet joined the SDG, whereas the following two were full salaries. The amount was about 300 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was this more or less than you were paid as a member of the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember the amount, this was about half the amount I received as a JATD member.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you paid in the same manner while you were a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard as when you were a member of the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We got our money in the envelopes, but the bank notes were brand new. And we were standing in line one behind the other with our rifles pointed at the one in front. And that's the way we would come up to the commander who would give us the envelopes with the salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Based on your experience with the Red Berets and the Serbian Volunteer Guard, who was in overall command of Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what I was able to conclude, it was a unit controlled by the state security of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On what do you base your statement that it was a unit controlled by the state security of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me first say that the staff of the Party of Serbian Unity in Belgrade was guarded by men with automatic weapons. And it wasn't possible or it wasn't allowed to use automatic weapons for that purpose without a special permission from the MUP. By the way -- or listening -- witnessing the communication between Legija and his superior, I was able to tell that he was subordinate to the one --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down and repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you were saying that something to the effect "By the way -- or listening -- the communication between Legija and his superior ..." Could you please continue.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. By the type of communication between Legija and our staff, it was clear that Milorad Ulemek was subordinate to them. The way that per diems were paid out in special envelopes only at these two places, then the use of long-barrelled automatic weapons to guard the headquarters of the Party of Serb Unity or the SDG in Belgrade, then the fact that uniformed persons were driving around in vans with a tiger insignia. These people were armed, driving around Serbia. All that tells me that this unit could not have behaved that way without the consent of the Serb police and the state security and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber. May I draw your attention to the fact that when I asked you not to ask questions on matters which are already in the statement, that the next three or four questions were exactly what we find already in the statement. And then you said you were almost finished. I hope that that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness provided greater detail than the -- than in his statement, and with the caveat that there's unresolved issue as to a substantial number of exhibits, that being the per diem records, the Prosecution doesn't have any further questions. But we would still reserve or express the caveat that there may need to be further discussion about those records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, do you think that the next break would bring you any further, or would it be a matter which the Chamber would have to deal with after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it would or would not, but the Prosecution is willing to discuss it with the Defence. It was a little hurried right at the end coming back here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll hear from you after the break. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I have to formally put on the record that P485 which is one of these photographs is admitted into evidence, that was not yet clear. Then, Mr. Weber, I don't know whether you've forgotten about it, but we haven't heard any summary of the 92 ter statement. I don't know whether you prepared it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I did prepare it. Pursuant to the Chamber's instructions of 18 February, 2010, I am ready to proceed with one. I didn't know, because of the fact he is testifying publicly, if you would want one, but I'm ready to proceed with one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the purpose is to inform the public about the evidence which is not elicited viva voce from the witness but nevertheless to enable the -- at the same time, of course, we've heard quite a lot of detail. I don't know how long it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's three and a quarter paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps we first hear that so that the public is better able to follow the proceedings. Have you explained to the witness what the purpose of this is?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I had not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll do it. Mr. Sliskovic, Mr. Weber will read a summary of what the public has not heard, which is the content of your statement. The public heard some details but not the main body of it. And in order for the public to follow the proceedings, Mr. Weber will briefly summarise it. It's not evidence. You don't have to correct it. But he will read it out. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The witness Dejan Sliskovic is a Serb male and former member of the special anti-terrorist unit of the Serbian DB. This unit of the Serbian DB is referred to as the JATD and commonly known as the Red Berets. Mr. Sliskovic was recruited into the JATD by a local head of an RDB centre in Pancevo. The witness went to the Serbian DB headquarters at Kneza Milosa Street 103 in Belgrade and Dragan Krsmanovic interviewed the witness after he underwent a medical check and psychological tests. Subsequent to this testing and interview, the witness reported to the Serbian KB headquarters in Belgrade and received an official decision confirming his employment with the Serbian DB. This decision was signed by Jovica Stanisic. Mr. Sliskovic was then sent to the Serbian DB facility in the Lipovica forest where he received training as a member of the Red Berets. The witness's instructors included Vaso Mijovic, Fica Filipovic, Zoran Rajic, and Drasko Suvara, among others. During his time in the Red Berets, the witness learned that these individuals were members of a paramilitary combat unit since the formation of Captain Dragan's training camp at Knin in 1991. Mr. Sliskovic travelled with other members of the regular formation of the JATD in a convoy. This convoy was joined by reserve/paramilitary formations of the Red Berets and also Arkan's Tigers who were under the command of Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic. Upon their arrival in Petrova Gora, the witness was deployed to guard the facilities where Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic were located. While on duty, Mr. Sliskovic saw Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic conduct a number of meetings. The meetings were held with Milan Martic, Fikret Abdic, Milorad Ulemek, aka Legija, and Stojan Zupljanin. In the spring of 1995, Mr. Sliskovic was sent to Tara and served under the command of Zvezdan Jovanovic as a member of the Red Berets. The witness subsequently left the Red Berets and later joined the Serbian Volunteer Guard, also known and referred to as the SDG or Arkan's Tigers. As a member the SDG, Mr. Sliskovic was sent to a base near Erdut. As a member of the SDG, the witness was paid in the same way as when he was a member of the Red Berets. In addition to the official decision of appointment signed by the accused Jovica Stanisic, Mr. Sliskovic's employment with the Serbian DB as a member of the JATD is confirmed on 25 separate per diem payroll records between the dates of June 1994 and July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Finally, one little detail. As far as geographical names are concerned, Mount Tara is familiar to the Chamber, Petrova Gora is, Lipovica is, I think that it's the first time that we have this location, but if the parties agree that it's approximately 20 kilometres south of Belgrade, is that where we found Lipovica forest?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness did talk about that in his statement. I didn't lead any evidence on it. I can lead it, but that is our understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's okay. Then there's no problem in relation to that. And who will be the first Defence counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, yes. First I have to inquire as to whether any solution has been reached on the documents you were discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The short answer to that is no. The witness on the stand is a witness who is able to authenticate a substantial number of records from the state security service of Serbia. Before tendering the witness, the Prosecution plans on tendering a total of 65 per diem and payment records from the state security service. It is our understanding based on the objection and concern that was raised by the Defence of Mr. Stanisic that there were transliterations of some but not all of the per diem records that were provided on this past week. The Prosecution acknowledges that this is the case. The Prosecution also would note that the Defence has notice of these names in two forms: First, the accused were provided with all of these exhibits in a language that is understood by them. The Simatovic Defence itself understands Cyrillic. Second, the additional transliterations that were tendered were just transliterations of the names, the remaining names that were listed in these exhibits. These names are also listed on different exhibits that were completed in complete translations. So the Prosecution did inquire with the Defence if there are particular names to which they feel there is a prejudice. There are no names that have been provided to us. Hence, the Prosecution would seek to proceed in this way: If there is no objection to the relevance or authenticity of this witness, with the witness on the stand with these 65 exhibits, then that is a matter that the Prosecution can tender the witness and we can deal with issues of notice as to whether or not there are any new or additional names which would seek to cause any prejudice to either the accused in written submissions. However, if there are any objections as to the relevance or authenticity of these documents, we do have a witness here present in the courtroom who has provided lengthy comments on 25 of the exhibits to which he has personally listed. As indicated earlier, these are per diem and payment records received pursuant to an RFA that's now in evidence as P469. In addition, there are detailed discussions as to the authenticity of these records in P470, the confidential annex from Serbia. We would submit to the Chamber that the similar names, stamps, format, and signatures that are present on the 40 non-associated exhibits convey a sufficient reliability upon those documents to warrant their admission at this time without further testimony of the witness. So we tender the floor to the Chamber with regard to this issue and the Defence; do not know if it's acceptable to the Defence, if there's an issue as to the notice of the new names that were transliterated, if they would raise it within a reasonable period of time in a written submission we can deal with it in that matter; otherwise, if there is no objection to the relevance and authenticity, we can tender the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- any response? Mr. Bakrac, you are the one who is said to be able to read Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I indeed am able to read Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, do you have any objections against the bar table admission, more or less, of the series of documents that -- the long series which we find on our list, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There are 25, they are associated and highlighted in green, and then there's an additional 40 that would be bar tabled. But the witness is likely capable to testify to their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection against any of these documents, and if so, on what grounds?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I have no objections. Albeit, I think that it may be convenient to ask this witness whether or not he had seen such lists before his testimony at all and whether he is familiar with them or whether he may have seen similar lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is discussed in the witness's statements for eight pages between page 18 and page 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, lots of numbers are -- is there anything in addition to what is already in the statement, Mr. Bakrac, that you would like the witness to tell us about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was mentioned, but, believe me, I'm not sure whether he commented what was shown to him or if he said that he remembers those lists to be a payroll. That is what I don't understand from his statement. My learned friend Mr. Weber indeed discussed these lists. I meant that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What then remains is whether he has seen this for the first time now or whether he had seen it in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, as it's indicated in the first one, he signed it and recognised his own signature on the document. So it seems very clear since his actual physical signature is on the document, it may not be in the statement whether or not he saw it before, but he indicated he signed the document, so I think there's an indication that he has physically been in contact with the list before. The other ones were signed by other individuals, and I think he's clear throughout his statement that he saw lists like this one, he either signed them or saw other people sign them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bakrac, if there's any additional question you'd like to put to the witness in cross-examination which is not already clear, then you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, you are right. That's what I will do. I apologise, my learned friend reminded me, it is mentioned in the statement that he recognised his signature on some of these lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jordash, the -- I think we identified the issue on which your objection was based at the beginning of the testimony as being one of notice. What you said, if I remember well, is that you had some of the names were transcribed in the Roman script but now having received all of the names transcribed in Roman script, you expressed some fear that now the Prosecution would deal with the other names as well. Now, I do not know exactly what was in the Roman script before and what was added last Friday. If there's anything -- that seemed to be the issue. Now, you've heard the testimony of the witness and you've heard the questions of the Prosecution. Is that still the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That is still the issue. We don't know, because we haven't had time to check, as in the Defence, what has been translated and what is new. The Prosecution say, Well, the names that have been translated which you were newly notified of on Friday don't prejudice you but we have no way because of the shortness of time of knowing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's just assume that you would not have received that on Friday. What would have been your position then?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, our position would have been that the Prosecution had notified us of the evidence that they sought to rely upon. They translated it. We had proceeded on that basis for the last months and years that this is the evidence which is the case against the accused. That in Cyrillic is not evidence because it's not in the working language of the Court. We will not look at that because our resources are limited and we look at what is the Prosecution case as notified by that which has been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what I do understand is that the Prosecution says, well, apart from the names we have given to you, There are others on that list; that's all. Is there -- do you want to research whether these others were not at home or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the big -- the issue in a way starts before this. What the Prosecution - and we've raised this before - what the Prosecution are doing is simply throwing names at us on lists and saying these are the people who were in the JATD. And when witnesses then come to testify in lengthy proofing sessions, as this witness himself underwent, a meaning is put on the name. So we have a name in the list, a witness comes along and says, Oh, yes, I remember that name; he did X, Y, and Z.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, now, has that happened here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any names which were in the earlier versions not readable for Mr. Jordash and Mr. Knoops on which you have asked questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Not that I am aware of. With respect to these exhibits, there are a lot of exhibits, and they are very extensive lists. Now, some of them are in Roman, some of them are in Cyrillic. So the Defence has the names in the Roman and they repeat in the Cyrillic and vice-versa. So they've been aware of the names. It's just now that we've completed the tranliteration of the -- of certain -- we just completed the tranliteration of the ones that were in Cyrillic. So that is our position. Again, not hearing any objection to authenticity of these records, which, by the way, we're not saying that they are members of the JATD, the Republic of Serbia is. And the Republic of Serbia is saying that they are member of the state security service. So the relevance of it seems quite clear. The authenticity seems quite clear. The Prosecution's wanting to deal with the issue of notice. If the Defence wants to put in writing in a short period of time how they are prejudiced, we can respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Jordash, authenticity or relevance, is that an issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, dealing with authenticity, in terms of the threshold employed by the Tribunal, probably not. Although it would be useful for us to be able to check those translations of the names to be sure. That's the first point. We would like to be able to have the same opportunity to independently verify, come to our own conclusion as to authenticity, as the Prosecution have had. They've had that opportunity. They served the new translations on Friday. They stand there saying, well, they're not prejudiced as to authenticity and relevance, and we cannot come to that same independent view ourselves. So that's authenticity. In terms of relevance, we are in the same place. And I go back to what I said a moment ago. The relevance is becoming apparent only witness by witness, and that's why we are taking quite a cautious view. When we have suddenly a new name translated from Cyrillic, it is not just the new name that is going to be a problem, it is going be the new name plus a new piece of evidence given by the next witness who is asked to comment on that name and asked to say whether he recognises that name or not and what that person on that list did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's for the future. What we have as relevance now is that we have lists of people that were apparently paid in a certain system. Those lists this witness appears on. Now if -- as soon as another witness would come and say, Oh, look, look, my name is on them as well, I do not see what the relevance issue is. I can imagine that you say relevance becomes a different one. That is, that we have to further explore and further investigate that name on that list. But at this moment those names who are on those lists where we have not heard any specific evidence either by this witness or by any other witness at this moment, it's just remaining names on lists, which lists are apparently records of payments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But without any proper, in our view, explanation as to relevance to the charges. Relevance as to the existence of the JATD, we can concede that. Of course, if they are put forward as lists relating to payments to JATD members, then they are relevant to that issue. As to relevance to the charges --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But isn't the existence of the JATD to some extent relevant for the charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So, therefore, we can't say that there's no relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we don't say there's no relevance, just not sufficient relevance indicated by the approach the Prosecution are taking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll deal with the matter. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber invites the Prosecution to tender these documents as bar table documents. If the Chamber -- the only possible concern the Chamber will honour is that notice has not been given to the Defence on the relevance of those other names in view of testimony still to be heard or evidence still to be presented. The -- although the Chamber considers that this is rather a matter of weight to be given to that evidence, the Chamber will, upon recent submissions, will give an opportunity to the Stanisic Defence, if in further investigating names that now suddenly are readable, although they were readable already for the Defence at an earlier stage in Cyrillic, but upon now investigating names which the Defence rightly or wrongly understood as not to be focused on because they were only given in Cyrillic, then we'll hear any recent submissions and find a remedy, or at least we'll consider whether any remedy is needed then. We do not urge the Prosecution to go through the whole of the list. That seems to be not efficient. And the Chamber, therefore, rather, proceeds in the most efficient way. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On the 23rd of November, 2009, we've had a pending bar table motion for all these exhibits now for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I don't know if the Chamber want us to re-file this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What -- of course, what would like to know is where these all of them. I hope you understand that I haven't got them all in my memory, exactly all the numbers. Is this -- there are more on that list?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There are some more. Actually listening to everyone in the courtroom, we're not very far apart. The Chamber hit it directly on that this is relevant to show the existence of the JATD, the Red Berets, that they existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least I asked Mr. Jordash whether he said -- he said the level of relevance is insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And Mr. Jordash then expressed a concern as to untransliterated names that are suddenly going to come out of the woodwork as being, I guess, perpetrators. But the Prosecution translated originally the key names to its case, so we are relying on these extra names as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're doing is arguing again your position at this moment, isn't it? Whereas the Chamber when I said you are invited, perhaps I should have said that the Chamber does not insist on going through those documents any further with this witness and at the same time gives an opportunity to the Prosecution where -- to the Defence who says, Well, we are not put on notice. But the annexes to the bar table submission, were all the names already written? They were not written yet in Roman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just wanted to add on. I didn't mean to interrupt, Your Honour, just because it didn't sound like we were actually that far apart on our perception on the documents. With respect to the record that we have right now, would Your Honours like me to formally read in the 65 ter numbers of the other 40 or just make that a part of the submission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would make that -- if you'd put that on paper and make that submission, a written submission, so we have them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And before tendering the witness, is there a ruling as to the objection as to the authenticity and relevance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was -- as matters stand now, there is no -- there is a challenge to the authenticity which is of such a general nature that the Chamber will deny at this moment such a challenge. But, again, if from the full list of names in the script you can read suddenly matters would appear differently, then, of course, the Chamber will hear from Mr. Jordash. As far as the relevance is concerned, the level of relevance which was considered by Mr. Jordash to be insufficient and in that respect he more or less contradicted himself that he said that under the case law of Tribunal it might be relevant material, that to the extent that the level of relevance is considered by the Defence to be an obstacle to admission, that is denied. Are matters clear for all the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender the witness with the understanding that we do have a witness on the stand that can testify to the authenticity or relevance of any of these documents. So absent any particular objections to any of these individuals, we tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take -- I take it that if the witness could tell us anything -- and the Chamber is not -- of course, authenticity, the Chamber can, under the rules, can require evidence of authenticity as it may be clear to you now that the Chamber is not requiring that, but, of course, if there's any challenge to the authenticity which goes beyond what we just heard, then Mr. Jordash and Mr. Bakrac have an opportunity to see whether this witness could give any evidence which should -- which would shed light on the possible lack of authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And it's just the Prosecution's understanding there's no objection from the Simatovic Defence to the admission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, as far as I understand there is not. Then I think we are ready to proceed. Who will be the first to cross-examine the witness? Will it be the Stanisic Defence? Mr. Knoops, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sliskovic, you will now be examined by Mr. Knoops. Mr. Knoops is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. Please proceed, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I please have P484 on the screen. P484.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Photographs usually take a while to be uploaded, and I think it was a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's my recollection that P484 was number five out of the series of -- or number 4, is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: It was the first photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the first photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. 6870A, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are almost there. Yes, there we are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this photograph you testified on earlier, was this taken before or after you were given your red beret?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived at the Tara camp after Operation Pauk, this is when the photo was taken. And when we were in our rooms, we usually wore our civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. So the answer to the question is that this photo was taken after you were given the red beret; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: This photo was taken approximately a year after I was given my red beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. And you agree with me that the red beret is nowhere on this picture amongst the equipment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: No, you can't see a red beret in the photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: But this room was really not very neat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the red beret itself, if it's still there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you do us a favour and put this red beret on your head? Yes, thank you, you can take it off. Is it correct, Mr. Witness, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the record could just reflect the red beret fit on the witness's head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, this is, I think, an interpretation of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree that what happened in Court should be put on the record. I leave it to you, Mr. Knoops, to describe whether it fitted or not or -- but on the record it's not visible now whether he did what you asked him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, maybe then the record can reflect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do not know -- I would easily do it myself If I would know what exactly it is what you would put on the record. He did put the beret on his head, and the lower part of the beret was to the right side of his head. To the right side. Now, I do not know whether what other relevant features you noticed which you would like to have on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That's sufficient, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, is it correct that the insignia on the red beret was put on the beret by yourself or by any of your family members?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I put the insignia on the beret the moment I was given both the insignia and the beret. The only thing that I changed later on were the screws on the bolts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So it is correct that when you were given the red beret it was without insignia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: No. All unit members were allowed to put their insignia on their berets. There is a place on the beret where you are supposed to put the insignia, on the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Mr. Witness, did you receive the beret and put the insignia yourself on the beret, on any occasion?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Fifteen of us put the insignia on our berets at the same time. I myself put the insignia on my own beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. And who gave you this insignia?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: At the Lipovica forest camp we received insignia together with the uniforms and the berets. And it was the man who was in charge of the storeroom who gave all those to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: The same accounts for the red beret, you got it through the storage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Myself and everybody else in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Until what time you had this red beret in your possession?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: That red beret was in my possession until six years ago when I handed it over to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Witness, that the red beret in your submission was given to you before the training?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, two days after arriving at the Lipovica forest camp, we were given the equipment. And that's when we also received the berets and the insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: At that time you still had to undergo the training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the beginning of training at the Lipovica forest camp and at Surcin Airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So actually the red beret was not a kind of a reward you got after the training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was part of the uniform that I was issued with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You are familiar with the fact that in those days there were many units wearing red berets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were also units in the military who wore red berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Witness, also the special -- 72nd Special Brigade of the VJ which you joined in 1995 had red berets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the fact that a unit with the name Mice wore red berets as well as the Wolves from Vucjak and the Predo units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that other units also wore red berets, but I am sure only of my unit and the 72nd Special Brigade from Serbia, I'm sure of these two that they wore red berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Witness, everybody in those days started to wear red berets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection. Vague as to the characterisation of everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it everybody is everybody in Serbia. Is that what you intended to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Including military units, paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So apparently you wanted to ask, Mr. Knoops, whether the witness agrees that in the police and military units that it had become customary for a large number of people not belonging to the units that were just mentioned to start wearing red berets. That's what you would like to hear from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And if I may add, if the witness could agree that the red beret in those days was not a symbol for elite unit anymore. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection. It's a compound question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question suggests that the red beret was once a symbol of an elite unit and lost that significance. Now, could we split up the two questions. Was, in the early days, was the red beret a symbol of an elite unit, Mr. Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is still the symbol of an elite unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did it lose that significance? And if so, when, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that it has lost that significance. The 72nd and the 63rd Brigades wore red berets. Infantry had green berets. Anti-aircraft units wore black berets. What I'm saying is that not everybody in Serbia could or was allowed to wear red berets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you agree that paramilitary units such as the Wolves from Vucjak, Predrag's unit, Mice, et cetera, were considered to be elite units?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that they were perceived as elite units. Wolves from Vucjak were considered an elite unit. But I can't tell you anything about any of the other units that you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Would you agree if paramilitary units would start to wear red berets that you would not qualify those units as elite units? Can you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: No, as a matter of fact, I said that when I joined the unit there were people there who had already been members of the Red Berets, which means that it was their honour to wear a red beret. It would not have been appropriate or fair towards them if they had been denied that kind of attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, but you did not -- you weren't part of such an elite unit before you came to this unit, isn't it, especially because you came from the Military Post 1205 where you worked as a logistics employee; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: You are right. However, I was not the one who decided on assigning or issuing red berets, and I really don't know why they were issued to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that later. Could you please tell the Court what the difference is between the red beret you were just handed and the red beret you apparently received when you served in the 72nd Special Brigade? Could you tell us what the difference is between those two red berets, please?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the manufacturer was different. One set was manufactured by factory Zarko Zrenjanin in Vuca, and I don't know about the other set. In any case, the shade of the red was different. That may have been due to the fact that some were newer than the others, but in any case, they were manufactured by two different factories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct that the insignia were the same?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: What insignia? In the 72nd Special Brigade, the insignia were different. The latter insignia that I was issued as a member of the anti-terrorist unit of the Serbian MUP was different, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So you are saying that there was a difference in colour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Some berets differed from others. Some were a bit darker, some were a bit lighter, but I suppose that that was down to the supplier. In those units, especially in military units, there was a high level of fluctuation among men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Would you agree that everyone in those days, and I mean then everyone, literally, could buy a red beret for storage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you could buy red berets. I believe that you can still buy a red beret in the same colour, that is available commercially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please describe the colour of the red beret of the SDG, as you mentioned that Mr. Legija wore a red beret?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Volunteer Guard did not wear red berets. I saw only Legija and Sarac wearing red berets, and those red berets were more or less the same as mine. The only difference was the trim around the border and the opening, their openings were different. But, in any case, the colour was the same. The colour of the beret was the same as the one that I wore while I was in Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yeah, you agree with me that you should be a professional to distinguish this band of the beret; is that true? Therefore, for a layman, an ordinary civilian, it was difficult or not possible to distinguish those berets; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: The colour was the same and within the unit different people wore different berets. Their sizes were different, and it also depended on the supplier. However, as you say, if a layperson looked at any of them, they would all look the same, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Including the number of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would finish this question, be aware that I'm looking at the clock at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, I know what you mean, Your Honour, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Including the number of air holes, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: There were air holes on all berets, two on each. There could not have been one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question is that I suggest to you that the red beret you just were given, was shown to the court, was actually the red beret you were give by the 72nd Special Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN SLISKOVIC
utterances.text: Was this a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sliskovic, what Mr. Knoops says that -- and he wants your comment on that, is that the red beret you just had in your hands was not the red beret you received at the beginning of your training in the JATD, but that it was the one that you received when you joined the 72nd Special Brigade. What is your comment on that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Knoops, in the last series of questions, you sometimes didn't just ask for facts but sometimes asked the witness's opinion of what he thought that others might be able to perceive, that is, double opinion and judgement rather than facts. I didn't stop you, although I could have done so. Could we try to focus on facts and not on what I think that the public would be able to observe as far as the difference of one or two little holes in the berets concerned. Of course, we are interested to know whether there are differences, but how it is perceived is another matter. We will adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 19th of May, at a quarter past 2.00 in this same Courtroom II. But, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Chamber hasn't given the customary warning to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. I've forgotten to do that. Mr. Sliskovic, we'll resume tomorrow, but I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony and not -- it's not only speaking to no one, but not to communicate in whatever way with whomever about the testimony, either testimony already given today or still to be given tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
